A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MindSearch framework. All text, equations, tables, figures, and end matter support comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendices; v2 includes readable Appendices A–G.

before.justification: v1 reports original closed-set QA experiments in Table 1 and a human-preference evaluation using 100 queries and five experts in Figure 4.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, component ablations, timing measurements, model generalization results, and error-recovery examples.

M1.justification: Section 2 retains the same DAG construction through Python code, hierarchical retrieval, parallel WebSearchers, and parent/root context propagation. Appendices E and G document error handling and system prompts without establishing a revision to the underlying procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate open-ended web QA, Bamboogle, MuSiQue, and HotpotQA. The new timing study still concerns researching and answering web questions; additional model configurations and selected failure examples extend analysis within the existing task coverage.

E2.justification: v1 compares against no-search and ReAct baselines, plus Perplexity.ai Pro and ChatGPT-Web for human evaluation. v2 adds evaluated self-ask, CodeAct, and Searchain comparisons on HotpotQA in Table 4, and explicitly compares ReAct, CodeAct, and graph planning with a common WebSearcher in Table 2.

E3.justification: The original evaluation settings are retained, but v2 adds controlled planner/searcher ablations, normalized inference-time comparisons with a ten-interaction limit, and a human timing protocol distributing ten questions among five experts. Appendix D also evaluates DeepSeek-V2, Qwen-2.5-7b, and GLM4-9b backends. Appendix F's annotation-interface details are additional disclosure, not evidence that the original human evaluation changed.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's illustrative trajectory comparisons, v2 adds planner and searcher ablations in Tables 2–3, inference-cost analysis in Figure 6, hop-count versus DAG-depth analysis in Table 5, and query-count analysis in Appendix C. Figures 7–9 add cases of code-error correction, unsuccessful-search recovery, and termination when information remains unavailable.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, variability estimates, or significance tests for model performance. The retained five-expert majority-vote evaluation and newly described assignment/shuffling procedures do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 1 and Figure 4 retain their original values. New results include HotpotQA averages of 58.3 for self-ask, 61.3 for CodeAct, and 61.6 for Searchain against MindSearch's 64.0, plus searcher-ablation scores of 60.6, 63.3, and 58.0. v2 also adds backend, graph-depth, query-count, and error-recovery findings; Appendix B reports 19h17min of human work versus 23 minutes for MindSearch.

T1.justification: The DAG definition G(Q) = ⟨V, E⟩ and its node/edge interpretation remain unchanged. Neither version provides theorems or proofs, and v2's graph-depth analysis is empirical rather than a new formal derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: graph-based multi-agent web search improves information integration, response depth and breadth, and competitiveness with proprietary search applications. The efficiency and human-preference claims are retained; new supporting experiments do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of inference scaling, DAG depth, query efficiency, and error recovery, and explicitly acknowledges incomplete citation-quality evaluation and lack of visual inputs or interactive browsing. Section 3.1.2 reframes factuality relative to breadth using the unchanged 70% versus 83% preferences. A new interpretive inconsistency appears in Section 3.3.2: it calls multi-query generation most influential, although Table 3 shows the largest removal effect for page selection.

D1.justification: Appendix G supplies both agents' system prompts, graph API documentation, output conventions, and citation requirements. Appendices E–F disclose error handling and annotation procedures, including randomized response order and the labeling interface. These substantially expand reproducibility information. The code link remains, while v1's model-availability statement and project-page link are omitted; this does not establish actual resource withdrawal.

R1.justification: v2 makes targeted additions concerning CodeAct, ReAct, Searchain, test-time scaling, additional language models, and web agents. Appendix A explicitly contrasts Searchain's chain regeneration with MindSearch's incremental planning. The original tool-use, RAG, and web-agent positioning remains largely intact.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are retained. v2 adds experimental subsections and organized appendices, expands the conclusion into 'Conclusion and Future Work,' makes local wording corrections, and updates title, author, and publication-header text. This is an extension rather than extensive rewriting or reorganization of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 2–6, Figures 6–10, and formatted response and prompt boxes. It translates Figure 5's labels into English, relocates that figure alongside Figure 4, and adopts a different conference layout and typography. Figures 1–4 retain their underlying visual content, while the new displays substantially expand the presentation.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked controlled evidence separating graph planning from generic code execution and identifying individual searcher components' contributions. v2 addresses these deficiencies through Tables 2–3, adds stronger comparator coverage, and supplies prompts and evaluation details that materially improve reproducibility. Cost analyses and explicit limitations further strengthen assessment of the unchanged method. These gains outweigh the new Table 3 interpretation error, although repeated-run uncertainty remains unreported.
